summary: This note describes adult contemporary (AC) radio programming, covering its audience targeting, its distinction from Billboard's Adult Contemporary and Adult Top 40 charts, and its history from the mid-1950s middle-of-the-road format through the soft rock peak of the 1970s to later consolidation around hot AC. It also notes the format's related subgenres and alternative names, and the artists associated with each.
one_line: Overview of adult contemporary radio format, its charts, audience, subgenres, history, and notable artists.
key_facts: In 1996, Billboard created the Adult Top 40 chart, which reflects programming between adult contemporary and pop music.
The Adult Contemporary chart and the Adult Top 40 chart are separate charts, and songs reaching one might not reach the other.
AC radio often targets the 25–44 age group, the demographic that has received the most attention from advertisers since the 1960s.
Fleetwood Mac's Rumours (1977) was the best-selling album of the decade.
By 1977, New York's WTFM and NBC-owned WYNY had switched to an all-soft rock format.
Michael Bublé and Josh Groban started out as AC artists.
Country musicians such as Faith Hill, Shania Twain, LeAnn Rimes and Carrie Underwood have had success on both AC and country charts.
When rock and roll became popular in the mid-1950s, many conservative radio stations wanted to play current hits while shying away from rock.
Middle of the road ("MOR") stations frequently included older pre-rock-era adult standards and big band titles.
In its early years the smooth jazz format was considered a form of AC, and George Benson, Kenny G and Dave Koz had crossover hits on both smooth jazz and soft AC stations.
Other names for the format include "Warm", "Sunny", "Bee" (or "B") and, particularly in Canada, "EZ Rock".
KOST originated the tagline that soft AC stations brand themselves as stations "everyone at work can agree on".
Beginning with the 2005-2007 economic downturn and eventual recession, most AC stations went for the more chart-based CHR, top 40, urban and Latino formats.
The rhythmic oldies format focuses primarily on "old school" R&B and soul hits from the 1960s to the 1990s, including Motown and disco hits.
Rhythmic oldies stations still exist today but target African-Americans as opposed to a mass audience.
